body:
What is SONAR?

SONAR stands for Sound Navigation and Ranging.

Sonar is a technology that uses sound waves to detect or obtain information about objects and features underwater.

Sound is particularly useful underwater because it can travel through water over substantial distances.

Sonar has applications in measuring water depth, detecting underwater obstacles and locating submerged objects.

Working principle of active SONAR

Active sonar works on the principle of sound reflection, or echo-ranging.

In the basic school-level example, a sonar device uses a transmitter and a receiver.

  1. The transmitter sends a pulse of sound, commonly ultrasound in echo-sounding applications, into the water.
  2. The pulse travels through water towards an underwater object or the seabed.
  3. Part of the sound is reflected when it encounters the object or seabed.
  4. The reflected sound returns to the receiver as an echo.
  5. The time between transmission and reception is measured.
  6. The distance is determined using the speed of sound in water and the measured time interval.

The frequency used by a sonar system depends on its application. Sonar is a general term for sound-based underwater detection and is not limited to 1 particular frequency.

Distance calculation using SONAR

Consider a ship using sonar to measure the depth of water directly beneath it.

Let:

  • v = speed of sound in water.
  • t = time between transmission of the pulse and reception of the returning echo.
  • d = depth of water.

The sound travels from the ship to the seabed and then returns to the ship.

Therefore, the total distance travelled is 2d.

\(2d = vt\)

Hence:

\(d = \frac{vt}{2}\)

Measuring sea depth

A ship transmits a sound pulse that returns from the seabed after 2 seconds.

Assume that the speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s.

\(d = \frac{1500 \times 2}{2}\)

\(d = 1500\,\mathrm{m}\)

The seabed is 1500 m below the ship, assuming the sound travels vertically and the stated speed is suitable for the calculation.

The total distance travelled by the pulse is 3000 m, but the measured depth is only 1500 m.

Active SONAR and passive SONAR

Sonar systems are commonly classified as active or passive according to whether they transmit their own sound.

FeatureActive SONARPassive SONAR
Sound emissionTransmits a sound pulseDoes not transmit its own pulse
DetectionReceives reflected echoesListens to sounds already present
Basic functionEcho-ranging and underwater detectionUnderwater sound detection and monitoring
Distance measurementCan use pulse travel timeCannot directly use a transmitted-pulse echo formula

Passive sonar can provide information about an underwater sound source, but a single passive receiver does not obtain distance by measuring the return time of its own emitted pulse because it emits no such pulse.

Important applications of SONAR

  • Water-depth measurement: Echo sounders determine depth from the seabed's reflected sound.
  • Seabed mapping: Sound measurements help identify underwater hills, valleys and other features.
  • Underwater navigation: Sonar can help detect obstacles and submerged hazards.
  • Object detection: Sonar can be used to locate sunken ships and other underwater objects.
  • Fisheries: Acoustic instruments can help detect groups of fish underwater.

Application in Gujarat

Gujarat has extensive coastal and port activities for which information about water depth and underwater features is important.

The Gujarat Maritime Board has a Marine Survey Sub-Division responsible for hydrographic surveys of ports and other water bodies. The Board identifies single- and dual-frequency echo sounders among the instruments used for this work, according to its official description available at the content cutoff of 3 November 2026.

A hydrographic survey measures and describes features of a water body, including water depth. An echo sounder uses reflected acoustic pulses to obtain depth information.

This is a practical Gujarat application of the same echo-ranging principle used in the school-level sonar example.

Connecting the important sound concepts

Sound begins with vibration and requires a medium for propagation. In air, it travels as longitudinal pressure variations. Frequency primarily determines pitch, while amplitude strongly influences loudness. Sound speed depends mainly on the medium and its physical conditions.

Reflection can produce a distinct echo or contribute to reverberation. Frequencies below 20 Hz are infrasonic, approximately 20–20,000 Hz is the normal human audible range, and frequencies above 20,000 Hz are ultrasonic.

Ultrasound supports medical imaging, industrial inspection and some underwater echo-ranging applications. Sonar uses the principles of sound propagation and reflection to obtain information about underwater objects and distances.

Prelims focus

  • SONAR stands for Sound Navigation and Ranging.
  • Active sonar emits sound and detects returning echoes.
  • Passive sonar detects sound without emitting its own pulse.
  • Echo-ranging distance is calculated using \(d = vt/2\).
  • SONAR is used for water-depth measurement and underwater detection.
  • Gujarat Maritime Board identifies echo sounders among the equipment used for hydrographic surveys.
  • Trap: The time measured in active sonar echo-ranging is the total outward and return travel time; the distance to the reflector is half the total sound path.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, section 12.5.1, SONAR, printed pages 171–172; NOAA National Ocean Service, What is sonar?, sections Active Sonar and Passive Sonar, updated 23 September 2026, consulted 3 November 2026; Gujarat Maritime Board, Nautical, section Hydrographic Survey of GMB Ports, consulted 3 November 2026.]
